# No Power at All / Key Stuck in Ignition 2009 Cobalt

When a 2009 Chevrolet Cobalt presents with power flashing on for a single second before cutting out completely, followed by the ignition key becoming physically stuck, you are looking at a classic cascade failure involving the immobilizer system and the steering lock. This isn't merely an electrical glitch; it is a safety interlock that has engaged too aggressively or failed to disengage due to voltage starvation.

The sequence of eventsâpower flash, total shutdown, key jamâindicates that the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or Body Control Module (BCM) detected an unauthorized state before the starter could engage. In modern GM architectures of this era, the ignition switch is not a simple mechanical plunger. It sends distinct resistance-based signals to the PCM regarding its position: "Off," "Accessory," "Run," and "Start." When you turn the key, if the voltage supply to these sensing circuits drops instantly after the initial flash, the modules interpret this as a fault condition. To prevent theft or rollback attacks, the system engages the steering wheel lock mechanism via an actuator solenoid. If the electrical signal required to retract that lock never arrives because the main power rail collapsed, the key remains trapped in the "On" or "Run" position.

The root cause often lies in a failing ignition switch assembly itself, but specifically one where the internal contacts for the accessory/run circuits are burning out before the start circuit. As the contacts degrade, resistance spikes, causing voltage drop. The modules detect this drop, assume the key is being turned off unexpectedly, and cut power to non-essential systems (lights, radio, dash) while simultaneously triggering the steering lock actuator. Because the actuator requires a specific pulse width of 12V to release the lock, and the power has already been cut to the rest of the vehicle, the solenoid never fires.

From an engineering perspective, this is a race condition between the voltage drop threshold and the module's safety timeout timer. The modules are programmed to lock out steering if they see more than one voltage dip within a specific timeframe. Once that dip happens, the system enters a "Safe State." In this state, power is diverted away from the ignition circuitry to save energy and prevent arcing, but the mechanical lock remains engaged.

Attempting to force the key out by wiggling it while applying pressure to the steering wheel often works temporarily. This manual override bypasses the electronic solenoid by mechanically releasing the tumblers. However, this is merely a workaround; the underlying hardware failure persists. The next time you attempt to start the car, if the ignition switch contacts fail again, the same sequence will occur: flash, death, and lock.

The definitive repair involves replacing the entire ignition lock cylinder assembly. It is critical not to simply replace the key or the tumblers alone, as the internal electrical contacts are integral to the switch's ability to signal the PCM correctly. When installing a replacement, verify that the new unit provides the correct resistance values for each position. If the resistance deviates from the factory specification, the PCM may reject the start signal entirely, leading to an infinite crank mode where the starter spins but the engine never fires.

There is also the consideration of the steering column clock spring. While less likely to be the primary culprit given the specific "key stuck" symptom, a broken clock spring can cause similar electrical interruptions if it breaks the ground path for the ignition switch. Before condemning the whole assembly, check for continuity in the wiring harness leading into the lock cylinder. A corroded connector at the base of the steering column is a common failure point that mimics a bad ignition switch.

If you are working on a fleet vehicle or managing multiple units with similar symptoms, inspecting the connectors behind the dash for corrosion becomes a priority. The 2009 Cobalt often suffers from moisture ingress in these tight compartments. Cleaning the contacts and applying dielectric grease can extend the life of the assembly, but if the internal switch contacts are physically worn, replacement is the only viable solution.

For those looking to troubleshoot similar issues on other GM models from that generation, the diagnostic strategy remains consistent: check the voltage at the ignition switch connector with the key in the "On" position. If you see 0V after a few seconds of holding the key, the switch is failing internally. Do not rely on aftermarket bypass kits designed to disable the steering lock; these violate safety standards and can lead to legal liabilities if the vehicle is involved in an accident where the theft-deterrent system was intentionally compromised.

Understanding the interplay between the mechanical lock actuator and the PCM's voltage monitoring logic is essential for resolving this issue permanently. The "flash" you see is the final gasp of the electrical system before it goes limp to protect itself.
